planting.note: Plant small container divisions in spring in very well-drained, acidic, sandy soil in partial shade; pyxie-moss is a slow-establishing specialty plant of pine barrens and sandhills, best purchased as a nursery-propagated container plant rather than dug or divided from the wild, and it resents disturbance once settled.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, acidic, sandy soil in partial shade — the lean, fast-draining sand of a pine barrens or sandhill habitat, not ordinary amended garden soil; pyxie-moss is a tiny, evergreen, moss-like mat-forming native of the mid-Atlantic pine barrens and southeastern sandhills, with needle-like leaves that hug the ground closely and, in very early spring, an unexpected profusion of small white to pale-pink star-shaped flowers that can nearly cover the tiny mats before most other plants have begun growing. It is a genuine specialist, evolved for deep, dry, acidic, nutrient-poor sand, and performs poorly — or dies outright — in richer, moisture-retentive garden soil or heavy shade. Grown mainly by rock-garden and native-plant enthusiasts as a choice, slow-spreading groundcover for a lean, sandy, sunny-to-lightly-shaded rock garden or sand bed that mimics its wild habitat. Give it excellent drainage above all else, minimal fertility, and patience, since it establishes and spreads slowly.
sources: New England Wild Flower Society / Native Plant Trust

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; fragrant Chinese pachysandra spreads by stolons at a more restrained pace than common Japanese pachysandra, so it takes a bit longer to fill in.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; fragrant Chinese pachysandra is a lesser-known relative of the common Japanese groundcover pachysandra, with the same glossy, dark-green, evergreen foliage but a more refined, restrained spreading habit and, true to its name, small flower spikes tucked in the leaf axils in early spring that carry a light, sweet fragrance the common species lacks. It makes a dense, weed-suppressing evergreen carpet under trees and shrubs, slower to spread than Japanese pachysandra but generally considered a better-behaved, more garden-worthy choice for gardeners who want the same clean, glossy shade groundcover without quite as much vigor to manage. Water during establishment and any prolonged dry spells; once settled it needs little care beyond an occasional edge trim to keep it within bounds.

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Korean waxbells is closely related to the more commonly grown Kirengeshoma palmata but has a more upright habit and larger, more outward-facing flowers.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Korean waxbells is a refined woodland perennial with large, maple-like leaves on sturdy dark stems, topped in late summer and early fall with clusters of thick-textured, pale-yellow, shuttlecock-shaped flowers that hang slightly outward rather than nodding straight down, a subtle distinction from its better-known relative Kirengeshoma palmata that gives it a somewhat bolder floral presence. It blooms late in the season, when few other shade perennials are still flowering, extending color in the woodland garden into fall. It combines beautifully with ferns, hostas, and other moisture-loving shade perennials in a humus-rich bed that never dries out completely. Established clumps need little care beyond a spring topdressing of compost and consistent moisture through summer; cut old stems back in late winter before new growth emerges.

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil, including dry, poor, or rooty ground, in partial to full shade; broad-leaved butcher's broom spreads slowly by rhizomes and, unlike the common spiny butcher's broom, has soft, unarmed foliage safe to handle.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil, tolerant of dry, poor, or root-filled ground, in partial to full shade; broad-leaved butcher's broom is an unusual evergreen shade shrub whose apparent 'leaves' are actually flattened, leaf-like stems called cladodes, broader and softer than those of the common spiny butcher's broom (Ruscus aculeatus), and — unlike that spiny relative — pleasant and safe to handle. Tiny greenish flowers appear directly on the surface of the cladodes in late winter, and on female plants pollinated by a nearby male, these are followed by bright red berries that persist attractively through much of the year. It tolerates deep, dry shade under mature trees better than almost any broadleaf shrub, spreading slowly by rhizomes into a low, dense, glossy-textured colony that needs essentially no maintenance once established. A useful, unusual evergreen for the most difficult dry shade in a woodland or shade garden, valued by flower arrangers for its long-lasting cut foliage.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Chinese sweetshrub is less cold-hardy and less fragrant than the American Calycanthus floridus but bears much larger, showier flowers, and benefits from some wind and afternoon-sun protection.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade with some shelter from strong wind and the hottest afternoon sun; Chinese sweetshrub is a striking relative of the familiar American Carolina allspice, bearing much larger flowers — broad, white-to-blush, waterlily-like blooms with a yellow-streaked interior — in late spring, a dramatic step up in size and showiness from the smaller maroon flowers of the American species, though with only a light fragrance rather than the American plant's strong spicy scent. Glossy, deep-green, oval leaves turn a clear yellow in fall. It is somewhat less cold-hardy than American Carolina allspice and appreciates a sheltered woodland-edge position rather than full, exposed sun. A choice, uncommon specimen shrub for a partly shaded border, valued more for the size and elegance of its individual flowers than for fragrance. Prune only lightly after flowering to shape, since it blooms on the previous year's wood.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in acidic, consistently wet to seasonally flooded soil in full sun to partial shade; sandweed grows naturally in Gulf South pine flatwoods ponds, bog margins, and ditches and tolerates standing water for extended periods.

directions: Plant in acidic soil that stays consistently wet to seasonally flooded, in full sun to partial shade; sandweed is a native wetland shrub of Gulf South pine flatwoods ponds, bog margins, and roadside ditches, with narrow, needle-like leaves and bright golden-yellow flowers with a prominent tuft of stamens blooming through summer. Older stems develop attractive reddish, peeling, exfoliating bark that adds winter interest after the leaves drop, giving the plant its 'peelbark' common name. It tolerates standing water for extended periods better than almost any other flowering shrub, making it a genuinely useful choice for the wettest part of a rain garden, pond margin, or low spot that floods after storms and stays soggy for weeks. Pollinators, especially bees, visit the flowers heavily through the long summer bloom season. Once sited in appropriately wet, acidic ground it needs very little care.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Himalayan hydrangea grows into a substantial large shrub to small tree over time and needs room to reach its mature size.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Himalayan hydrangea is a large, vigorous shrub to small tree from the Himalayan foothills, producing broad, flat lacecap flower clusters in creamy white in early summer, larger and often earlier-blooming than many familiar garden hydrangeas. As the shrub matures over several years, the bark begins to peel and flake in attractive cinnamon-brown patches, giving it worthwhile winter interest well beyond its bloom season — a feature few other hydrangeas offer. Its eventual large size makes it best suited to a woodland-edge planting, the back of a large shrub border, or as a specimen with high, filtered shade from taller trees, rather than a small foundation bed. It flowers on the current season's growth, so any pruning to control size or shape is best done in late winter before new growth begins, without sacrificing that year's bloom. Water regularly during establishment and dry spells, since hydrangeas wilt quickly when the soil dries out.
